title.en: Where AI Actually Belongs in an SFU Stack

description.en: AI can improve SFU operations without owning packet routing: a bounded control-plane design for WebRTC, LiveKit, NATS, and QoE signals.

content.en:
AI is moving into real-time media infrastructure, but “AI-driven routing” is often too vague to be useful. In an SFU stack, the difficult question is not whether a model can produce a routing recommendation. It is whether that recommendation can be trusted inside a latency-sensitive data path where one unstable decision affects an entire room.

My preferred design is conservative: keep packet forwarding deterministic, use AI to interpret telemetry and predict pressure, and place a policy controller between model output and production actions. The model advises. Explicit software constraints decide.

That separation matters more than the model choice.

## Start with the proven media path

In the WebRTC architecture I worked with, LiveKit handled interactive media and NATS JetStream connected control-plane events. HLS was used only for delayed playback available hours after the session, not as a scalable live-viewing path. The system supported 5,000 concurrent users.

AI was not the reason for those results. The important decisions were architectural: separate interactive participants from passive viewers, avoid forcing every audience member through the expensive WebRTC path, and keep control-plane coordination independent from media forwarding.

That baseline changes how I evaluate the current AI trend. I would not replace a working SFU scheduler with a probabilistic model. I would add intelligence around the scheduler where uncertainty is useful and failure can be contained.

## “AI routing” hides several different problems

Routing inside a real-time media system can mean very different things:

- Selecting which video layers a subscriber should receive
- Choosing an SFU region for a new participant
- Detecting when a node is approaching saturation
- Moving a room before quality degrades
- Prioritizing an active speaker under constrained bandwidth
- Deciding when viewers should use WebRTC or the HLS path

Some of these decisions happen for every packet or subscription update. Others happen when a participant joins, a room grows, or an operational threshold changes.

The distinction is critical. A model should not sit synchronously between an incoming RTP packet and its forwarding decision. That path needs predictable execution time, simple failure behavior, and enough observability to explain why a packet was dropped or forwarded.

AI is more appropriate for slower control loops: capacity forecasting, anomaly classification, room-placement recommendations, and analysis of quality-of-experience signals. Those outputs can improve the system without becoming a hard dependency for media delivery.

## Put intelligence beside the data plane

I would divide the architecture into five parts.

### Deterministic media data plane

The SFU remains responsible for receiving, selecting, and forwarding media. Existing rules enforce bandwidth limits, subscription permissions, simulcast or scalable-video layer selection, and congestion responses.

If every AI component disappears, this layer must continue operating with its last safe configuration or its normal deterministic defaults.

### Telemetry pipeline

SFU nodes publish structured observations: packet loss, jitter, round-trip time, available bitrate, layer switches, keyframe requests, room size, CPU pressure, and egress behavior.

NATS JetStream is a good fit for transporting these events because producers do not need to wait for model inference. Durable consumers can process observations independently, and replay is available when a classifier or policy is changed.

The event stream must be sampled and aggregated carefully. Sending every packet-level observation to an AI service would create a second scaling problem beside the media platform itself.

### Model services

Different problems should use separate models or statistical methods rather than one general “routing AI.” Examples include:

- Classifying whether quality degradation is network-, codec-, or node-related
- Forecasting node pressure from room growth and recent bitrate behavior
- Detecting unusual layer-switching or retransmission patterns
- Ranking candidate regions for a new room
- Summarizing correlated incidents for an operator

A conventional forecasting model may be better than a large language model for capacity. A rules engine may outperform both when the signal is clear. The architecture should support the simplest technique that meets the operational requirement.

### Bounded policy controller

Model output enters a controller that validates recommendations against hard constraints. It checks capacity, region eligibility, privacy requirements, room affinity, migration cooldowns, and the maximum amount of change allowed in one control cycle.

This controller is the safety boundary. It can reject a confident but invalid recommendation, require repeated evidence before acting, or downgrade the action to an operator suggestion.

### Audit and feedback store

Every recommendation should retain its input window, model version, confidence, policy decision, resulting action, and observed outcome. Without this history, teams cannot distinguish a useful model from one that merely produces plausible explanations after normal system behavior.

## Useful applications that do not own packet forwarding

Capacity prediction is a strong starting point. CPU utilization alone is usually a lagging signal in media systems. Room composition, subscribed layers, publisher bitrate, recording, and egress workloads can indicate pressure before a node reaches a hard threshold. A model can combine those features and recommend safer placement for the next room.

Quality-of-experience classification is another practical use. A rise in packet loss can originate from the client network, an overloaded SFU, a bad regional route, or a mismatch between available bandwidth and the selected layer. Classification can help the controller choose between reducing a layer, avoiding a node, or simply collecting more evidence.

Operational triage is also valuable. Correlating SFU telemetry, NATS events, deployment changes, and regional incidents is time-consuming. AI can group related symptoms and produce a concise hypothesis for an engineer. It should link to raw evidence rather than pretending its explanation is ground truth.

Media intelligence belongs on a separate decoded branch. Transcription, moderation, scene analysis, and caption generation require access to decoded media or an appropriate derived stream. They should not be described as free metadata processing inside a non-decoding SFU. Forking selected streams to dedicated workers keeps expensive inference away from the forwarding path and makes consent, retention, and scaling easier to manage.

## Protect the latency and failure budgets

An AI component introduces network calls, queueing, inference variance, model-version drift, and new failure modes. Those costs need explicit budgets.

For join-time placement, a recommendation can be computed from recently aggregated state before a participant arrives. For live adaptation, the system can consume asynchronous recommendations and apply them only if they are still relevant. Stale advice must expire automatically.

Timeout behavior should be boring. If a model is unavailable, the controller uses deterministic placement and adaptation rules. If confidence is low, it observes without acting. If recommendations oscillate, cooldown and hysteresis rules prevent rooms from bouncing between states.

This is also why direct model control of the hot path is a poor default. Real-time systems already have difficult feedback loops. Adding a probabilistic controller without rate limits and stability constraints can turn a small prediction error into repeated layer changes, unnecessary migrations, or synchronized load movement across nodes.

## Evaluate decisions, not model demos

A convincing prototype should be tested against operational outcomes rather than a polished dashboard.

Start by replaying historical telemetry in shadow mode. Let the model produce recommendations without changing production behavior. Compare those recommendations with actual incidents, deterministic scheduler choices, and the decisions experienced operators made.

Then run a constrained canary where the controller can perform only low-risk actions. Measure whether it detects pressure earlier, reduces avoidable quality degradation, or improves node utilization without increasing instability.

The evaluation should include adversarial cases:

- Missing or delayed telemetry
- A sudden room-growth spike
- Conflicting signals from client and server metrics
- A model service timeout
- A recommendation based on a node that is no longer eligible
- Repeated contradictory recommendations

The most important result is not raw prediction accuracy. It is whether the complete decision system produces better outcomes while preserving predictable fallback behavior.

## Cost needs the same discipline

The hybrid system controlled cost by matching transport to audience behavior: WebRTC for interaction and HLS for scale. Adding AI should not quietly erase that advantage through permanent GPU allocation, excessive telemetry retention, or unnecessary inference on every room.

Inference should therefore be selective. Run expensive media models only for streams that need them. Aggregate control-plane signals before classification. Use lightweight statistical methods for stable numerical problems. Reserve larger models for tasks where unstructured context actually matters, such as incident summarization.

Cost attribution should be visible per capability. If AI-assisted placement reduces overload but costs more than conventional headroom, the comparison should be explicit. “AI-powered” is not an architecture metric.

## A practical adoption sequence

I would introduce this design incrementally:

1. Standardize SFU and client telemetry with consistent room, participant, node, and region identifiers.
2. Build deterministic dashboards and alerts before training a model; unclear data does not become clearer through inference.
3. Replay telemetry through a shadow classifier or forecasting service.
4. Add a policy controller that can validate and log recommendations without acting.
5. Enable a narrow, reversible action for a small canary population.
6. Compare operational outcomes, rollback behavior, and total cost against the deterministic baseline.

This sequence creates useful infrastructure even if the model fails to justify production control. Better telemetry, explicit policies, replayable events, and decision audits improve the platform on their own.

## The engineering principle

AI can make an SFU platform more adaptive, but reliability comes from where the model is placed and how little authority it receives by default.

Keep media forwarding deterministic. Move inference to asynchronous control loops. Validate every recommendation through explicit policy. Preserve a complete fallback path. Measure decisions against real quality, stability, and cost outcomes.

The strongest AI-enhanced media architecture is not the one with a model in every component. It is the one that uses uncertainty where it adds information and keeps certainty where the system cannot afford surprises.
